job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

response.passage: Teacher: Today, let’s discuss how percentages work in real life. Rohan, if a shopkeeper offers a 10% discount on a shirt marked at ₹500, how do we calculate the final price? Rohan: I think we just take 10% of the selling price, so it would be ₹50. Teacher: Actually, discount is always calculated on the marked price, not the selling price. Now, Priya, if an item’s price increases by 20% and then decreases by 20%, is the final price the same as the original? Priya: Yes, it returns to the original price because the percentages are equal. Teacher: That is a common mistake. The second 20% decrease applies to the new, higher price, so you lose more than you gained. Also, remember that percentages can represent values larger than 100%, such as a 150% increase in production. Finally, when calculating simple interest, always ensure the time is in years. If the rate is yearly, you cannot simply plug in months; you must convert them to years first. For instance, six months is 0.5 years. If you use months directly, your interest calculation will be completely wrong. Always be careful with your base values, as they determine the accuracy of your entire calculation.
response.summary: This passage explains that discounts are calculated on marked prices and that percentage changes are not reversible. It also clarifies that percentages can exceed 100% and that time must be converted to years for interest calculations.
